title: Man shot during fight with officer at traffic stop dies
subtitle: Const. Jeff Blair, who was stabbed in the neck, is expected to recover.
article: The man who allegedly stabbed Toronto police officer Jeff Blair in the neck during a traffic stop late Sunday has died in hospital after he was shot by the patrol officer during the altercation.
Peter Lumanglas, 38, of Toronto was shot during a traffic stop the area of Northmount Ave. and Delhi Ave. in North York around midnight.
Both men were taken to Sunnybrook hospital with life-threatening injuries.
Lumanglas was pronounced dead Friday at 10:35 a.m. A postmortem is scheduled for Saturday morning, the provincial police watchdog agency, the Special Investigations Unit, said in a news release.
The SIU has assigned six investigators and three forensic investigators to probe the circumstances of this incident.
At various times during the week, Lumanglas teetered between life and death as police waited to see if they would be able to lay charges, according to a source.
In an interview with Global News this week, the suspect's girlfriend, Krystle Magallanes, said she was shocked to hear the news of the shooting.
"They're saying Peter was shot and stuff, and when they said he stabbed a cop, I said no way," she said.
"Of all my time knowing Peter, there's no way, he's not that violent," Magallanes told Global TV.
Const. Blair fired off several shots. It is not known how many struck Lumanglas.
Blair required surgery but is now in stable condition and expected to make a full recovery.
Lumanglas was the father of a 5-month-old baby and just finished an eight-month sentence for drug trafficking last New Year's Eve, according to Global.
"I'm uneasy about everything because I know that the last time he got out of jail, he told me he just really wanted to be a good father," Magallanes explained.
Blair, a husband and father in his 30s, is a patrol constable with 13 Division and has 12 years of service with Toronto police.
"It will be a slow period of recovery," Police Chief Bill Blair said in a YouTube statement.
"His family is with him and, of course, he has a tremendous outpouring of support, not only from his colleagues in policing but from the people of Toronto."
"He was on his own enforcing the law," said the chief, who is not related to the injured constable.
Quick medical care on the scene and in hospital was credited for helping pull the constable through.
Mike Salb, a Toronto firefighter for 22 years, had been watching the evening news and getting ready for bed with his wife, Renate, when he heard, "Stop, police!" Then, five gunshots rang out.
From his window, Salb saw Const. Blair slumped against his cruiser. The officer then fired two more shots, he said.
Salb called 911 and rushed outside to help Blair, who was bleeding from a deep gash to his neck.
Wearing a Toronto Fire T-shirt and identifying himself as an emergency responder, "I approached the officer and he asked me to secure his gun."
After taking the gun inside his home, the off-duty firefighter grabbed paper towels, gloves and a flashlight and went back outside to help treat Blair's injuries.
He stayed with the officer, applying pressure to his wound for about five minutes, until paramedics and more police cruisers arrived.
During that time, the other man involved in the altercation was lying face-down on the ground, Salb said.
"My first thought was to aid the officer . . . It's a little unnerving, for sure," he said.
